articles.title: 'There's babies in there': Hero dad who stopped Oregon school shooter shares his story
articles.summary: Kaylub Giamanco, the man praised as a hero for fatally shooting a gunman at a school in Bend, Oregon, last week, is speaking out for the first time about the moments leading up to the shooting and how he is grappling with the aftermath. The 36-year-old carpenter, whose two daughters attend Silver Rail Elementary School, told Oregon Public Broadcasting that it was happenstance that he was passing by the school at that moment. He said he had decided to go home for lunch that day instead of eating the food he had packed. As he drove by the elementary school, he saw a "man in black" holding a long gun and shooting at a vehicle. At first, he thought it was a prank, but then the shooter threw the gun over the school fence before climbing it. "That's when panic fled into my brain and that's when I opened my center console and said, 'No. No. No. No,'" Giamanco said in the interview. In the console of his truck was a .40-caliber handgun he rarely used. He said he grabbed the weapon's magazine from another compartment, drove into the school parking lot and saw the shooter walk across school grounds. "I just was in full panic, like, 'No, there's children, there's babies in there,'" he recalled. "I told my Siri to call 911." He said the dispatcher had questions for him, but he didn't stay on the call. "I said, 'I'm sorry, I have to go in. People are going to die,'" Giamanco said. He described trying to stay out of sight as he followed the gunman. "I heard him fire two shots into the doors," Giamanco said. "That's when I started hearing children pleading for their lives and then I started hearing gunfire and I just started army crawling faster and faster and I told myself this is probably the last thing that I'm ever going to do." Giamanco said he crawled in through a broken window, staying on his knees until he reached the special education classroom. He said he saw a teacher struggling with the shooter. He said he swung the door open and fired. "He (the shooter) was scrambling for his weapon," Giamanco said. "I looked at him and I shot him two more times to make sure that he couldn't move because I was afraid of him shooting anybody else." Oregon Gov. Tina Kotek was among those who praised Giamanco's bravery, saying he "heroically intervened to stop further loss of life." Police Chief Mike Krantz also credited the teacher who tackled the shooter and fought to take his gun, which "almost certainly helped prevent more bloodshed." Police later identified the shooter as 16-year-old Griffin J. John II. The attack killed three children , ages 5, 8 and 11, and a 25-year-old teacher. A 7-year-old girl and a 54-year-old teacher were wounded. "I didn't save everybody. I didn't get them all." After police and first responders arrived at the school, Giamanco went back to his truck, emptied his weapon and called his wife and then his mother. "She was just like, 'OK, baby, calm down. You did the right thing. You're a hero. You saved lives.' And I was just like, 'I didn't save everybody. I didn't get them all,'" he recalled of the conversation with his mom. His mother, Kenda Freeman, who lives in California, told CBS News Sacramento that her son "has a genuine heart and he loves his community and his family and his children." A week later, Giamanco told Oregon Public Broadcasting that when he goes to bed at night, he replays that day in his head and wonders if he could have stopped the shooter sooner. "I relive, I see faces, I hear voices, I hear screams," he said. "It was split-second decisions while gunfire was going off, while children were losing their lives." He grew emotional when talking about the families who lost children. "I want to apologize for not saving their babies," he said. "The gratitude for saving people's children is awesome, but there were ones that I didn't save." In the days after the shooting, Giamanco sought to avoid the limelight, putting out a brief statement expressing gratitude to first responders and the community. However, he told Oregon Public Broadcasting he's now decided to share his story. "I've always wanted to change the world, but I've felt small. I'm just a carpenter from Bend, Oregon. I was a nobody other than to my friends and family," he said. "I feel like if I'm going to have a voice, then I'll be damned if I'm not going to use it to change this world, to make it a better place." He said he hopes to help raise funds for local schools to improve their safety. This article originally appeared on CBS News at https://www.cbsnews.com/news/hero-kaylub-giamanco-bend-oregon-shooting/

articles.title: Judge rules Jane Doe in Cornell case can remain anonymous while pursuing lawsuit
articles.summary: A judge in New York on Friday decided the former Cornell University student known as Jane Doe can pursue her sexual assault claim against the university and seven fraternity members while remaining anonymous. Permission to proceed in litigation under a pseudonym is not automatic, but the judge said "the notoriety of the allegations and widespread reports of certain malicious actors' behavior" warranted anonymity. Jane Doe says she felt 'unsupported and disbelieved' by Cornell president The judge's decision came with a warning to those who have threatened Jane Doe and others connected to the case. "While the Court is cognizant that some members of the public have made it their mission to try and identify Jane Doe, and have likewise tried to use what they believe to be Jane Doe's identity to harass and threaten certain individuals allegedly tied to her, the Court issues the following words of caution: cyberstalking and engaging in or encouraging threats across state lines, whether it be of Jane Doe, any of the named defendants, or their attorneys, can be considered a federal crime and perpetrators of those acts may be subjecting themselves to prosecution," Judge Phaedra Perry-Bond wrote in her opinion. Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images - PHOTO: A hand written sign is seen before a rally in support of a former Cornell University student known as Jane Doe at the Ithaca Commons, October 13, 2026 in Ithaca, New York. Former Cornell fraternity president dropped from Jane Doe lawsuit Jane Doe filed a civil lawsuit alleging she had been drugged and gang-raped at the Chi Phi fraternity house in October 2024. All seven men named in the lawsuit have denied wrongdoing and no criminal charges have been filed in the case. Her attorney, Thomas Giuffra, has previously told ABC News that Jane Doe and her family have been subjected to threats, doxxing and other forms of harassment. New York Attorney General Letitia James, who was appointed by Gov. Kathy Hochul, is conducting an investigation into the incident. Cornell, which said it fully supports the appointment of a special prosecutor, is also conducting an internal probe of its response to the allegations. The case has rocked the university and started conversations about treatment of sexual assault allegations on college campuses across the country. Cornell has said it takes allegations of allegations of sexual violence "extremely seriously" and that it "investigated and adjudicated the allegations consistent with university policies." At the same time, the university has said it is committed to taking additional steps to improve campus safety. articles.title: Ukraine says Starlink restrictions remain despite Trump's claims they're lifted
articles.summary: Watch: Who controls Ukraine's access to Starlink? Ukraine is still recording issues with the Starlink internet network, sources within the defence ministry say, after Donald Trump said limits had been reversed by Elon Musk who owns the satellite system. The sources told the BBC that instances of drones experiencing connection loss at speeds of 161km/h (100mph) were being recorded, hampering military operations. The US president had denied instructing the tech billionaire to restrict connectivity to Starlink's military-grade counterpart, Starshield, before saying on Thursday that Musk had "put it back". Asked on Friday, Trump said: "If there is a problem, I will get it straightened out." Trump added: "I have not spoken to him. I might have to, but I have not. I've heard it was fixed, but if it's not, I'll speak to him." Musk previously said he was not behind the slowdown, which affected Ukraine's ability to use attack drones and co-ordinate defensive operations. Trump told reporters he did not think the tech billionaire had too much power. The Ukrainian defence ministry sources said the military was constantly monitoring the performance of both the Starlink and Starshield networks. They added that there was "currently no confirmation that these restrictions have been lifted". Last week, Kyiv said uplink speeds to the low Earth orbit satellites had been restricted, affecting the speed at which drones could travel. Any drone travelling faster than 100mph lost its connection, officials said. Shortly after, Musk said that Starshield , which Ukraine uses for some of its operation, was controlled by the US military and suggested that the Pentagon could be behind the issues. The White House has since repeatedly denied deliberately placing limits on the network in Ukraine. In a call with Trump on Friday evening, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham "underlined the importance for Ukraine to have full access to Starlink so they can continue to defend themselves against Russia's full-scale invasion", Downing Street said in a statement. Why is Starlink internet so important on the battlefield in Ukraine? Ukraine uses both the civilian service Starlink and the more secure Starshield, depending on what communications are needed. The networks use 10,000 satellites to provide connectivity, particularly in remote areas and on the battlefield. Starshield allows Ukrainian drone operators to see targets in real time, as well as operate interceptor drones. Russia is not authorised to use Starlink, so when Ukraine sends long-range missiles deep into Russia to hit oil refineries, the network does not work. One Ukrainian soldier said there was "simply no alternative" to Starshield, adding that earlier in the week, connectivity had been cutting out when his unit had been travelling in a car at 80km/h (50 mph). "I'll tell you this much: God forbid they shut it off completely - it would be an absolute catastrophe," he told the BBC. "We need a backup option for securing communications and internet." Another soldier said they had reverted to the "proven algorithms" they used before they had Starlink when it initially started playing up, but stressed that Ukrainian forces did need the network, citing its speed. "Even one or two seconds is critical when we can transfer data and orders faster," she said. "You can really feel that advantage on the battlefield." Ukrainian reports of a slowdown to the service came during a tense diplomatic row between Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky about Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil infrastructure. Faced with midterm elections next month, Trump has waived some sanctions on Russia and agreed a deal to import Russian diesel for the US market - a move criticised by Ukraine and its European allies. [BBC] Trump said the strikes on Russian oil refineries, which Kyiv says are crucial to stemming the main revenue source for Moscow's war effort, have pushed global prices higher. While the attacks have had an impact on global fuel prices, rises seen this year have primarily been due to the Iran war . Zelensky said the US had also threatened to withdraw intelligence sharing if the strikes did not stop, something Trump later denied. The row prompted a war of words between the two world leaders, with Trump suggesting it was time for Ukraine to get a new president and Zelensky implying Trump was not a real leader. Earlier on Thursday - before Trump's comments - Zelensky had said the speed of the system had still not been restored fully. "I am waiting to hear from US Secretary of State [Marco] Rubio. He promised to get back to me with information within 48 hours or so." The Wall Street Journal reported that Trump had told Musk that he was frustrated the Starlink system's speeds were still capped, and that the system was working closer to normal following that conversation. articles.title: Employee error blamed for toxic chemical leak that sent 60 people to hospital in Ohio
articles.summary: A chemical leak that sent 60 people to the hospital and forced hundreds of people to flee their homes has been blamed on an employee error. Mayor Wade Kapszukiewicz announced the cause of the tank leak at a news conference on Friday and said that all remaining evacuation orders in Toledo , Ohio . The chemical leak happened Tuesday night when an employee of MC Tank Transport “introduced a temperature level to the tank in the process of trying to transfer the liquid" that caused a chemical reaction, the mayor said. MC Tank Transport said the tank contained glycidyl methacrylate , which it described as “an industrial chemical used to make certain plastics, paints and coatings perform better.” A plume of smokes rises from MC Tank Transport Inc., where a chemical tank exploded overnight, prompting hundreds of residents to evacuate or shelter in place amid concerns about a potential toxic release, Wednesday, Oct. 21, 2026 (AP) The evacuation orders were lifted after the company finished venting the tank that ruptured. That allowed a hazmat team to enter the site and test safety levels. “At this time, we do feel confident that the site is safe," Toledo Fire and Rescue Battalion Chief Blake Molnar said. Dr Brian Kaminski, vice president of medical affairs for ProMedica hospitals, said about 60 patients were treated at the hospital, most suffering relatively minor symptoms. A small number of patients who had underlying health conditions were admitted, he said, and all patients were expected to recover. The company has “accepted responsibility” for what happened, the mayor said. The U.S. EPA on the scene near MC Tank Transport Inc. (AP) “There was no fire, there was no explosion. There was a very serious chemical reaction, which now happily has run its course, and we’re now finally able to return to some level of normalcy here in our community," he said. Based on data that officials have seen so far, the amount of the chemical in the air didn't reach levels high enough to have “a long-term meaningful impact on human health,” according to Kapszukiewicz. articles.title: Oil prices hit 6-month high over fears of escalating fighting in the Middle East
articles.summary: Oil prices climbed to a 6-month high on Friday as traders priced the odds of escalating fighting in the Middle East.  Attacks near the Red Sea also stoked worries of further constraints on oil supplies from the region. Brent crude ( BZ=F )  futures for December delivery settled at $116.72 per barrel. The international benchmark posted its third consecutive week of gains. Meanwhile, West Texas Intermediate crude ( CL=F ) closed just above $103 a barrel. President Trump telegraphed an escalation in Iran after the midterm elections and an extended stand-off, with the Strait of Hormuz remaining at the center of the conflict. This week, the New York Times reported that the US and Israel have reportedly drawn up plans for renewed attacks on Iran after the Nov. 3 elections. The US has ordered nonessential embassy personnel to depart Saudi Arabia after a series of attacks at the country's airports and oil fields . President Trump has said he will not attack Iran before the midterms and has suggested that fuel prices will fall afterward. Meanwhile, the Red Sea area has seen increased attacks recently, including on Saudi Arabian airports and on an Aramco oil field this week. Saudi Aramco on Thursday ordered the evacuation of its headquarters in Dhahran , marking the oil giant's first such evacuation since the Iran war began. On Friday, the national price of gasoline stood at $4.29 per gallon, roughly $1.22 higher than a year ago. Diesel hovered around $6.31, about $2.68 more than this time last year. A power outage at a refinery in the Chicago area is expected to send refined fuel prices even higher in the region. "You're going to see a lot of $5 gas prices in places like Michigan, Ohio, Minnesota, Illinois, and Indiana," Gulf Oil chief energy adviser Tom Kloza told Yahoo Finance on Thursday. Ines Ferre is a senior business reporter for Yahoo Finance. articles.title: Democrats are favored to flip the House, but Republicans still have a path to victory
articles.summary: It's crunch time. With less than two weeks to go until the 2026 midterm elections, Democratic and Republican candidates for the U.S. House of Representatives nationwide are making one last push to persuade voters in their districts — and help their party win or retain control of the chamber on Nov. 3. The stakes are high. President Trump has enjoyed complete Republican control of Congress for the first half of his second term. Flipping the House would give Democrats the power to block parts of the president's agenda, investigate his administration and even impeach him (again) . Historically speaking, a president's party almost always loses seats when voters return to the polls to judge his first two years in office. (The average number lost since World War II? Twenty-six .) Sometimes, the backlash is so pervasive that the president's party loses seats across a wide range of competitive districts — a phenomenon known as a "wave" election. But the past doesn't necessarily predict the future, and Republicans have certain advantages today that they didn't have before. Here's what needs to happen for each party to come out on top. Yahoo The races to watch The first thing to know about any House election is that while all 435 congressional districts are technically up for grabs, roughly 80% of those contests (representing about 350 seats) are not considered competitive. House incumbents have always had huge advantages: money and name recognition, mostly. But their head start has only widened in recent years as partisan polarization and redistricting have helped make the vast majority of congressional districts "safe" for one party . These days, incumbents tend to focus more on fending off primary challengers. The general election can be a breeze in comparison. As a result, this year's true battleground is relatively small. According to the nonpartisan Cook Political Report's " race ratings ," just 17 contests are genuine "tossups" at this point. Another 16 "lean Democratic," and 17 "lean Republican." There's also a third competitive category that includes 18 seats where Democrats are the "likely" winners, and 13 seats where the same could be said about Republicans. That's 81 competitive districts — again, out of 435. It's clear from looking at this year's ratings which party is playing more defense and which is playing more offense — and where. Only 30 Democratic seats are considered competitive, and more than half of them (17) are "likely" to remain Democratic, according to Cook. Just five Democratic seats are tossups. Just two are leaning Republican. In contrast, a full 51 Republican seats are considered competitive — and about half of them are tossups (12) or leaning Democratic (12). Geographically, this year's tossups are concentrated in certain kinds of places: Rust Belt districts in states that have swung from party to party in the past (such as Michigan, Pennsylvania and Ohio); Mid-Atlantic suburbs (in states such as New York, Virginia and North Carolina) where Trump has scrambled some of the usual coalitions; and Sun Belt districts (think Florida, Texas, California and Nevada) where Latinos factor heavily. Trump carried many of these areas in 2024 . On Friday, Cook shifted another 19 of its race ratings toward Democrats — part of a pattern that has seen the outlet move a total of 63 race ratings toward Democrats over the last month. "Republicans' path to keeping control of the House has all but evaporated," Cook's House analyst wrote . "Following this latest round of ratings changes, Democrats now are favored outright in the 218 seats they need to win control of the House. In other words, 220 seats are rated either Solid, Likely or Lean Democrat. Republicans, meanwhile, are favored in 198 seats, rated Solid, Likely, or Lean Republican." Overall, the map gives Democrats more pickup options — which means more paths to a House majority. The path to a Democratic House Senate and governor contests can be quirky — more state-specific and personality-driven. But national dynamics tend to play a larger role in shaping the composition of the incoming House. So it's not just a matter of who has more targets on the board. It's that the board itself tends to tilt to one side or the other, taking most of those targets with it. A recent example was the 2010 midterm election, when impatience with America's slow recovery from the 2008 financial collapse and frustration with President Barack Obama's response helped Republicans gain 64 House seats. Beyond the history of midterm backlash against the president's party, Democrats have two big advantages right now. One is that the current Republican majority is so minuscule — just 219 votes to 214, including an independent who caucuses with Republicans — that Democrats only need a net gain of three seats to win back the House. The other is that the board seems to be tilting in Democrats' favor — assuming the polls are right. Surveys suggest there's one underlying factor pulling the national electorate to the left: dissatisfaction with Trump. According to the data journalists at Silver Bulletin , an average of 60% of Americans currently disapprove of how Trump is handling his job vs. 37% who approve. That puts the president's net approval rating at -23% — near his all-time low. Trump is earning even lower marks on voters' top issue this year: the cost of living . Shortly after he returned to office, roughly equal numbers of Americans approved and disapproved of how the president was handling inflation. But today — as tariffs and the Iran war help drive prices up — 71% disapprove and 25% approve . That's a 46-point gap. President Trump arrives to speak at a campaign rally at F&M Bank Arena on Oct. 10, 2026, in Clarksville, Tenn. AP Photo/Alex Brandon Democrats aren't particularly popular. But for the party in power, it may be hard to overcome this level of dissatisfaction with the status quo. That's why, when pollsters ask their so-called generic ballot question — If an election for U.S. Congress were held today, which party's candidate would you vote for in your district? — Americans are currently giving Democrats a substantial lead of more than 9 percentage points , on average. Making matters worse for Republicans, that lead has grown over the last month as swing voters who favored Trump in 2024 — including some Latinos and independents — say they're planning to vote Democratic. To put a 9-point lead in perspective, Democrats were leading by an average of 7.6 points on the generic ballot at this point in 2018, with Trump as president and Republican majorities in the House and Senate. On Election Day, they picked up 41 seats and flipped the House. If the polls are right, Democrats might win control of the House again. The path to a Republican House But are the polls right? Recently, Republicans have pointed to some surprising survey results on the Senate side — including Democratic leads in rural red states such as Iowa , Kansas and Nebraska — to argue that pollsters might be misjudging public sentiment. They're not wrong to say the polls have missed in the past. Polling errors are commonplace; they happen in most elections. But they tend to be random and to change directions from one cycle to another . The Trump era has been a little different. In each of the three presidential contests that Trump himself has competed in, the final average of polls conducted before Election Day underestimated Republicans' performance in the popular vote by an average of 3.8 percentage points, according to data journalist Nate Silver . The theory is that a phenomenon called nonresponse bias — in which Democratic voters are more eager or available to respond to pollsters than Republican voters — might have made Democratic support look stronger than it actually was. Pollsters try to adjust for this by weighting their results — that is, using statistical methods to give less weight to respondents who are overrepresented demographically and more weight to respondents who are underrepresented demographically. But it's difficult to predict in advance who will show up on Election Day. This time around, there are signs that rural Republicans are not responding to pollsters in certain states . Could that mean Republican candidates in those places will outperform their polling? Possibly. But experts say it may also mean that rural Republicans are less supportive of the GOP than they were in 2024 — potentially voting Democratic or staying home on Nov. 3. A voter walks toward his polling place. REUTERS / REUTERS After all, there's been virtually no polling bias toward Democrats in Trump era elections when Trump himself wasn't on the ballot. In fact, the polls since 2016 have overestimated Republican support in midterm elections (by an average of 0.2%) and off-year, special and runoff elections (by an average of 1.3%), according to Silver . Either way, pollsters aren't seeing signs of this rural effect in most states — and even if they were, it might make only a minor dent in Democrats' 9-point national lead . Redistricting is the other Republican advantage. House redistricting efforts typically take place every 10 years, after each new census reveals changes in population distribution. But last summer, Trump successfully pushed GOP legislators in Texas to pass new congressional district boundaries five years earlier than normal to help Republicans win five additional House seats in 2026. This kicked off a tit-for-tat cycle that saw nine states adopt new congressional maps for the midterms — some to benefit Democrats, others Republicans. Now that the dust has settled, Cook projects that Republicans could win nine seats because of redistricting (in Alabama, Florida, Louisiana, North Carolina, Ohio, Tennessee and Texas), while Democrats could win five (in California and Utah). If that plays out, it would net the GOP four seats overall. It's not what Republicans initially hoped to gain from gerrymandering. "We're not gonna win all 13 of those redistricted seats. That's correct. We're not," GOP House Majority Whip Tom Emmer of Minnesota told Axios recently . But it's also not nothing. The hope for the GOP is that some combination of polling error and redistricting boost — along with a late influx of hundreds of millions of dollars to help defend districts Trump won in 2024 — will be just enough to preserve their slim House majority. articles.title: 2 former FBI officials charged with lying to Congress about Hunter Biden laptop probe
articles.summary: Jeanine Pirro, U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia.  (Aaron Schwartz / Bloomberg via Getty ) WASHINGTON — Two former FBI officials who have come under withering criticism from allies of President Donald Trump have been charged with allegedly lying to Congress over the investigation into former President Joe Biden’s son Hunter Biden . A court docket shows that Nikki Floris, the former deputy assistant director of the FBI’s Counterintelligence Division, and Bradley Benavides, another FBI official, were facing one count of the rarely-charged criminal offense which can be difficult to prosecute. Hunter Biden was investigated, charged and eventually convicted of  gun and tax crimes, before his father pardoned him shortly leaving office. U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia Jeanine Pirro said in a social media post that Floris and Benavides had surrendered Friday morning. She alleged that the duo lied about their roles in the Foreign Influence Task Force and “about their roles in the FBI’s Hunter Biden investigations.” Attorneys for Floris said in a statement that Floris was “a patriot” who “served our nation as a dedicated FBI intelligence officer for nearly 20 years” and was charged so the administration could “push a false narrative for a shot at political points.” Deputy Assistant Director for Counterterrorism at the FBI Nikki Floris testifies before the House Judiciary Committee hearing on Capitol Hill on Oct. 22, 2019. (Susan Walsh / AP) Attorneys Margaret Donovan, Chris Mattei, Mary Dohrmann and Kyle R. Freeny said in a statement that the “DOJ has accused her falsely of a crime on the say-so of politicians, not on the facts. It’s no coincidence the government is filing these nonsense charges now, years later, on the eve of an election.” One of the attorneys for Benavides, Ronald S. articles.title: Trump says he ordered lawsuit to potentially block certification of Alaska Senate race
articles.summary: President Donald Trump on Friday said he told his administration to file its lawsuit to block certification of the U.S. Senate race in Alaska if Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan loses, kicking off what many fear could become a lengthy battle between the government and states over certifying an election where the president's party is struggling. “I'm the one that said do it,” Trump told reporters as he landed for a campaign rally in Florida. The lawsuit, filed late Thursday, centers on one of the president's longstanding complaints in the Senate race — the presence of a second candidate named Dan Sullivan, who Republicans fear could siphon away votes from the incumbent in what's likely to be a photo-finish contest with Democrat Mary Peltola, the state's former congresswoman. The second Sullivan, who is Daniel J. Sullivan from the tiny fishing community of Petersburg , has said he decided to run on his own, but Republicans have contended he is a Democratic plant to siphon votes away from their candidate. The lawsuit by the Republican president's Department of Justice in federal court in Alaska demands that the state be blocked from certifying a Peltola win if Daniel J. Sullivan remains on the ballot. “The United States accordingly brings this lawsuit to protect the integrity of the 2026 Senate election in Alaska,” the lawsuit says. The legal challenge came 11 days before the Nov. 3 election and months after the final ballot was set. It is the latest example of the Department of Justice bolstering Trump's political operation, targeting his enemies and suing Democratic-controlled states before the election. Democrats and many voting rights advocates have long feared that the administration will try to block certification of elections that Trump’s party loses, much as he unsuccessfully tried to do when he lost the 2020 White House race to Democrat Joe Biden. The Alaska Supreme Court rejected a previous Republican effort to remove Daniel J. Sullivan from the ballot, and the state's Republican officials made the decisions about how to list him on the ballot. He will appear without a party designation next to his name, while the senator will be listed as the Republican incumbent. Alaska's ranked choice voting system also will allow voters to select both of the men if confused. Peltola and Sen. Sullivan were top vote-getters in nonpartisan primary The senator received more than 68,000 votes in the August primary, while the challenging Sullivan got 4,107, about 2% of the total vote. Peltola, who had previously served one term in the House, was the top vote-getter in the nonpartisan primary. Both parties expect that whoever wins in November will do so by a tight margin in a state of 738,000 people. The campaign for Sen. Dan Sullivan did not address whether the senator supports the Department of Justice's intervention. “We'll let the DOJ complaint run its course,” campaign spokesman Nate Adams said in a text message. “Alaskans can tell the difference between a Democrat sideshow and Senator Sullivan's strong record of delivering for Alaska.” Daniel J. Sullivan, whose presence on the ballot is at issue in the lawsuit, did not respond to a request for comment. “Donald Trump knows that Dan Sullivan is going to lose the election, so now his Department of Justice is filing a sham lawsuit to overturn the will of Alaska voters and steal an election when he loses,” said Devan Barber, executive director of the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee. Peltola, on her Substack, wrote, “This is a blatant, despicable political threat – all because a historically unpopular 12-year incumbent is scared that he’s going to lose the Senate seat that belongs to Alaskans.” In a statement Friday, the Department of Justice noted that Alaska's election officials, who are Republicans, determined the other Sullivan's campaign was an attempt to “mislead” voters and wanted him removed from the ballot. Both a state court and Alaska's Supreme Court disagreed and kept the second Sullivan on the ballot. "The Justice Department, consistent with the National Voter Registration Act enacted by Congress, is taking the necessary steps to ensure that this frivolous candidacy does not undermine the integrity of Alaska’s election or the will of its voters,” the department's statement said. Concerns about the Department of Justice's role in the election had already reached a fever pitch this month after it filed an unusual, last-minute lawsuit demanding California segregate ballots from 20,000 voters who the Trump administration believed could be noncitizens. California said that it appeared many of those identified were indeed citizens and that they had no time to carefully investigate, as the administration threatened to prosecute the state's election workers if there was illegal voting. U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche denied the action was a prelude to challenging certification of the midterm results in that state, adding that such a move may happen under a “doomsday” scenario but was unlikely. “It is not DOJ’s intention to, and it’s never our intention to, improperly interfere with elections or the state certification process," he told reporters Thursday in Virginia before the Alaska lawsuit was filed. The lawsuit was signed by Associate U.S. Attorney General Stanley Woodward, who represented Trump allies and Jan. 6 defendants before becoming one of the top appointees at the department. Constitution gives states the power to run elections Derek Muller, a law professor at the University of Notre Dame, said the lawsuit would likely only kick in if Republicans narrowly lose the Alaska Senate race and that it probably would not survive long. “The statute simply doesn't let the Department of Justice enjoin certification,” Muller said. “The lawsuit could well be mooted by a wide Democratic victory or a narrow Republican one, and if not, the court will likely dismiss it next month.” The U.S. Constitution grants states the power to run their own elections. Elections for federal office like the Senate must comply with standards set by Congress. That division of power has frustrated Trump, who repeatedly has tried to seize control of election procedures through executive orders that courts have blocked . The final step for a state election is formally certifying the winner, the act that the administration's lawsuit seeks to prevent, it requests, “pending an investigation to determine whether votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan were meant to be cast for Senator Sullivan." The process in Alaska is complicated by the state's ranked choice voting system, which Trump opposes, and many expect it to take weeks before a winner is known. Also on the state's ballot is an initiative to repeal that system. Trump has stepped up complaints about a ballot with dueling Sullivans Trump has complained about Daniel J. Sullivan's presence on the ballot, making reference to it during a rally in Alaska this month and in repeated social media posts, including one this week where he called it “CHEATING.” “We are looking at powerful legal options to remove the fraudulent Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. from the Ballot, and holding the Democrats accountable for their Election Interference, in the pursuit of Justice and Fairness,” the president wrote on Wednesday. Clogging a ballot with third-party candidates to siphon off votes from the other major party is a long-standing tactic in the country's two-party system. Republicans have been linked to an effort to persuade Ohio voters to support a socialist in that state's Senate race, which could help Republican Sen. Jon Husted fend off a challenge from former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown. ___ Associated Press writers Becky Bohrer in Juneau, Alaska, Ali Swenson in New York and Alanna Durkin Richer in Washington contributed to this report. articles.title: Kushner pushes back on report involving phone, spies, transfer
articles.summary: Jared Kushner is pushing back on a report involving a hacked iPhone, international spies and billion-dollar transfers from foreign governments. An upcoming book by journalist Matthew Cole claims Kushner, who is President Trump's son-in-law, had access to more than $2 billion in "slush money funds" from Middle Eastern leaders in an attempt to influence U.S. foreign policy. An excerpt of the book released Thursday details allegations encompassing Kushner's time as a senior White House adviser during the first Trump administration, which included a lead role in U.S. policy in the Middle East. Kushner had a major hand in negotiating key foreign policy deals that involved Israel, the Gulf states, China and Russia during that period. Kushner and his legal team released fiery statements Thursday night categorically denying all accusations against him. Kushner said , "The allegations made by this author are completely insane and never happened." His attorney called them "false and defamatory" and said they intend to pursue legal action against those responsible, but did not specify whom. The new book, "Princes and Thieves: Jared Kushner and Mohamed bin Zayed's Secret Plot to Remake the Middle East," alleges Kushner had access to billions of dollars in undisclosed foreign bank accounts intended to pay for "influence within the U.S. government." An excerpt from the book that was published in "Vanity Fair," but not independently verified by CBS News, says Dutch intelligence agents learned the Russians had hacked Kushner's iPhone in 2017 after flipping a Russian spy and subsequently gained access to Kushner's phone as well. According to the report, "when Kushner used the phone, they could see his screen. Almost as soon as they got inside, the intelligence service began capturing every image of Kushner's screen as he used it." At the time, Kushner served as a senior White House adviser to President Trump, including on Middle Eastern diplomacy. The report alleges Dutch spies witnessed him log into a United Arab Emirates account that had allegedly received hundreds of millions of dollars from a bank in Azerbaijan, and claims the leaders of Saudi Arabia and the UAE put at least $2 billion into multiple bank accounts linked to Kushner, including an account with Israel's Central Bank. According to the book excerpt, the owners and managers of the accounts were often disguised as official government entities or charities, but the funds were actually intended for "off-the-books diplomatic objectives" such as striking a deal to end the Israeli-Palesteinian conflict. The report also claims Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman put roughly $1 billion into at least one account for Kushner, citing a "person with knowledge of the money" saying "its allocation was for Kushner's personal benefit." Kushner forcefully denied the accusations leveled in the "Vanity Fair" excerpt, writing in part, "The allegations made by this author are completely insane and never happened." "We denied every claim on the record, yet the author provided not a single shred of verifiable evidence to substantiate them," he said. "No bank statements, wire transfer records, account numbers, transaction dates, or other verifiable details were provided to support these extraordinary accusations," he said. CBS News reached out to the White House, which referred us to a statement from Steven Cheung, who is assistant to the president and White House director of communications. Cheung said the "bull**** Vanity Fair article comes from a book that is complete fiction, and was fabricated from the warped mind of failed spy thriller writer." "He presents no evidence or even a shred of documentation. Just mysterious words from unnamed sources," Cheung said on X. articles.title: Melania Trump secures ceasefire in Russian-held Ukrainian city, White House says
articles.summary: First lady Melania Trump (Finn Gomez/Getty Images) First lady Melania Trump has successfully negotiated a temporary ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine to allow humanitarian aid and civilian evacuations in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian town of Oleshky, her senior adviser, Marc Beckman, revealed for the first time Friday on Newsmax's " National Report ." Appearing live in the Newsmax studio, Beckman disclosed that representatives of both countries had signed the agreement just hours before his appearance, marking a significant humanitarian breakthrough in the nearly five-year war. "Let me start by being very crystal clear: the first lady of the United States of America has successfully negotiated a ceasefire between Ukraine and Russia, localized in this region of Oleshky," Beckman told Newsmax. The ceasefire, scheduled to begin Oct. 29, will allow Ukrainian and Russian civilian representatives to enter Oleshky, about 5 miles behind the front lines, to identify residents needing assistance and coordinate evacuations, Beckman said. "It will bring humanitarian aid to the entire city, this includes medics, medicine, food, clean water," he said, noting the operation will include "an evacuation of the city of Oleshky as well." Newsmax has been granted exclusive television access to accompany a delegation of Russian and Ukrainian observers entering Oleshky on Oct. 29. Both Ukrainian and Russian officials agreed to allow Newsmax to document the humanitarian operation. Beckman emphasized the immediacy of the breakthrough, revealing that the agreement had only just been finalized. "As recently as this morning, I'm coming here, and the ink is still wet on the paper," he said. He said the agreement had been signed just hours before his Newsmax appearance. "So you're the first to know," Beckman said. Residents Facing Starvation Oleshky, located in southern Ukraine's Kherson region, had about 24,000 residents before Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022. Fewer than 2,000 residents remain, primarily elderly civilians unable to escape, along with approximately 50 children. Conditions have deteriorated dramatically, with residents facing severe food shortages, limited electricity, no running water, and no heat. Roads around Oleshky are reportedly heavily mined and targeted by armed drones. One route connecting Oleshky with nearby Radensk has become known as the "Road of Death" because it is littered with destroyed vehicles. Beckman described an increasingly desperate humanitarian emergency. "They're eating weeds and grass," he told Newsmax, describing reports of civilians struggling to survive. In a statement released Friday, Melania Trump said her intervention was essential to prevent further suffering. "The situation in Oleshky is dire. Oleshky is a front-line war city on the brink of disaster," the first lady said. "Oleshky's remaining population is comprised primarily of elderly residents who urgently need medical attention, medicine, food, and clean water." "It was abundantly clear that without my intervention, the possibility to bring humanitarian aid into the city and to evacuate the elderly would be impossible." Beckman revealed on Newsmax that the negotiations began after the first lady learned about Oleshky's humanitarian crisis during her Fostering the Future Together event held in conjunction with the United Nations General Assembly in September. Her earlier efforts to reunite children separated from their families during the war helped establish direct communication channels with Russian and Ukrainian leaders. The first lady has helped facilitate the reunification of 34 Ukrainian and Russian children with their families since the war began. "Both sides formally recognized her as an intermediary and in writing, and they gave her the power to negotiate this ceasefire," Beckman said. Beckman said the first lady spent more than a month negotiating with both governments to finalize the agreement. The first lady said representatives from both countries will visit residents in their homes, assess their needs, and arrange transportation for those wishing to leave. "Residents who wish to evacuate will receive coordinated support and transportation to their preferred destination," Trump said. "I anticipate some will want to go to Russia, and some to Ukraine." Newsmax cameras will document the operation, providing independent visibility into the evacuation process and whether residents' wishes are respected. A Possible Step Toward Peace Although the agreement is limited to Oleshky and does not establish a broader ceasefire, Beckman expressed hope that it could lead to further diplomatic progress. "Indeed, in my opinion, this is the first step towards everlasting peace between these two nations," he said. Beckman said Ukrainian and Russian representatives were enthusiastic when signing the agreement, saying both countries' presidents had supported the first lady's efforts. Nevertheless, he cautioned against assuming the humanitarian breakthrough would immediately produce a comprehensive peace agreement. "My hope is that this ceasefire... creates a better peace within the region for Europe," Beckman said. For now, the immediate priority remains delivering desperately needed supplies and providing a safe passage out of Oleshky. The unprecedented arrangement puts Melania Trump at the center of a rare cooperative humanitarian effort between the warring nations Important: Download the free Newsmax App on your smartphone and get latest updates from Ukraine, Russia and our breaking news! articles.summary: SK海力士放弃旗下Solidigm赴美IPO ，消除了NAND闪存市场一个潜在的供应扩张来源，美光科技与闪迪有望受益，但实际股价弹性仍受当前市场环境制约。 据LYNX Equity Strategies分析师团队10月23日发布的研究报告，若Solidigm顺利完成IPO，募集资金将用于在美国扩建NAND产能，可能在三年或更长时间后推升全球供应量，进而压制行业定价。如今这一融资渠道关闭，该风险已随之消散。 LYNX在报告中明确表示， 此次计划告吹对美光和闪迪"均属实质性利好"，两家公司同为NAND供应商，产能增长风险的降低有助于支撑行业定价与估值水平。 不过，分析师团队同时提示，当前市场环境可能限制两家公司股价的实际涨幅。 周五，美光收涨2.46%，闪迪收跌1.82%。 IPO取消切断产能扩张资金来源 Solidigm拟建的美国生产基地原计划由SK海力士与英特尔联合出资，选址可能位于英特尔的俄亥俄州园区。美国本土制造基地一旦建成，具备实现快速产能扩张的条件。 由KC Rajkumar领衔的分析师团队指出，此次IPO所对应的并非立竿见影的供应增量，而是三年乃至更长周期后的潜在产能释放。 上市计划搁置后，这一中长期供应压力的触发机制被切断，LYNX将其定性为"全球NAND闪存市场新增产能的潜在压力已被消除"。 美光与闪迪获供应面支撑，英特尔承压 对美光科技和闪迪而言，受益逻辑在于供应端的不确定性减少。NAND闪存属于典型的供需敏感型市场，产能规划的边际变化对价格走势影响显著。少了Solidigm美国产能这一潜在竞争来源，两家公司的定价空间理论上将获得一定保护。 英特尔则可能因此承受小幅负面影响。该计划的搁置意味着其俄亥俄州园区失去了一个潜在制造项目，对园区的利用规划形成一定干扰。 LYNX的分析同时强调，此次变化的本质是减少了未来潜在的竞争来源，并未立即改变当前NAND市场的既有供应格局。 美光科技和闪迪能否将供应面的改善转化为业绩与股价的实际提升，仍取决于行业整体产能规划走向以及供需关系的后续演变。 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。

articles.title: Instacart寻求出售，股价涨超9%！DoorDash在潜在买家之列，Uber退出
articles.summary: 杂货配送公司Instacart正在评估出售选项，包括与Uber及DoorDash进行的初步接触，消息一出Instacart单日大涨逾9%。 据彭博援引知情人士透露， Instacart近期曾主动接触Uber洽谈出售事宜，但Uber已退出谈判，双方目前不再进行讨论。 据The Information报道， Instacart正在评估潜在的出售计划，已与包括Uber和DoorDash在内的潜在买家进行了初步洽谈，并已聘请一家投资银行评估各类选项。 消息公布后，Instacart周五收涨9.21%，市值约134亿美元。与此同时，市场对潜在买家面临的反垄断风险及收购成本作出反应——Uber股价收跌3.4%，DoorDash收跌3.5%。 竞争压力下的战略抉择 Instacart探索出售的背后，是其在杂货配送市场日益承压的经营现实。 自2023年上市以来，该公司收入增速持续落后于主要竞争对手：2024年及2025年收入增速均放缓至约11%，而DoorDash去年的收入增速达到28%。 Instacart今年第二季度收入同比增长14%至10亿美元，自由现金流达4.80亿美元，财务基本面尚可，但在规模与增速上已明显落后于更具资源优势的竞争对手。 分析称， 若以科技行业近期并购惯例的30%至40%溢价计算，Instacart的收购估值约在160亿至170亿美元之间。 收购将面临严峻的反垄断审查 对于潜在买家而言，收购Instacart的战略逻辑在于将其成熟的零售商合作网络与买家自身的配送基础设施及用户体量相结合，以进一步巩固在美国杂货配送市场的地位。 值得一提的是，Instacart与Uber之间已存在商业合作关系，用户可直接通过Instacart应用程序订购Uber Eats。 然而， 任何一方的收购都将面临严峻的反垄断审查。此类交易将进一步集中美国最大的几家餐饮与杂货配送平台，监管层面的阻力不容忽视。 Uber的并购日程同样可能形成制约。据报道，该公司今年7月已宣布以近150亿美元收购德国外卖平台Delivery Hero，此外还涉及对ezCater的收购交易，多项并购同步推进或令其在出价Instacart时面临更大的整合与监管压力。 历史谈判的前车之鉴 这并非Instacart首次身处并购讨论之中。据The Information报道，DoorDash早在2021年就曾探讨以400亿至500亿美元的估值收购Instacart，彼时Instacart的私募市场估值约为390亿美元。 但那轮谈判最终破裂，部分原因正是双方对交易能否通过拜登政府的反垄断审查存有疑虑。 与2021年相比，当前市场环境已大相径庭——Instacart估值大幅缩水至约120亿美元，但反垄断监管的不确定性依然是悬在潜在交易上方的核心变量。各方谈判目前仍处于早期阶段，能否最终促成交易尚无定论。 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。

articles.title: 穆迪维持法国信用评级不变，负面展望持续
articles.summary: 法国在一场高度关注的信用评级审查中暂时躲过降级。 10月23日周五，穆迪宣布维持法国Aa3评级不变，为这个深陷债务压力、政治僵局与社会动荡的欧元区第二大经济体提供了短暂喘息空间。 穆迪在声明中指出， 法国多元化的经济结构与强健的公共机构支撑了现有评级，但同时将展望维持于负面，理由是政治不稳定性将持续制约财政整顿努力。 穆迪表示， Aa3评级的维持建立在法国最终通过削减赤字预算方案的基础假设之上，并预计"融资成本与社会紧张态势将在未来数月内有所缓解"。 此次决定对债券市场而言意义直接。此前市场已在相当程度上消化了降级预期，法国与德国10年期国债利差一度升至178个基点，触及欧债危机以来最高水平，法国10年期基准收益率也攀升至2002年7月以来高点5.14%。 穆迪维持评级的决定或有助于暂缓借贷成本进一步上行，但分析人士警告，鉴于财政与政治层面的深层隐患尚未解除，市场压力难以根本消散。 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。

articles.title: 特朗普威胁对伊朗发动小规模“史诗怒火”行动，伊拟打击海底电缆，霍尔木兹传油轮触雷
articles.summary: 美伊冲突持续升级之际，特朗普一边暗示可能再次对伊朗发动军事行动，一边释放战争可以迅速结束的信号。伊朗传出已制定计划，一旦战事重启就打击海湾地区海底通信电缆，地区能源运输与通信基础设施面临的风险同步上升。 据央视新闻，当地时间10月23日周五，美国总统特朗普表示，美国或许会再来一次小规模的“史诗怒火”行动，又或者伊朗会选择妥协。特朗普称，如果伊朗足够聪明，就会直接说：“咱们来谈正事吧。” 同在周五，伊朗伊斯兰革命卫队海军称，当天两艘试图非法穿越霍尔木兹海峡南部的超级油轮触雷。伊方称，两艘油轮共载有超过450万桶原油，船员弃船逃生。这些说法尚待独立核实。 对国际能源市场而言，当前最重要的变量仍是霍尔木兹海峡能否维持稳定通行，以及美伊冲突是否进一步扩大。特朗普的表态显示，美国仍在军事施压与结束冲突之间权衡。伊朗方面有关油轮触雷及海底电缆打击计划的消息，则进一步凸显了冲突升级可能带来的多重风险。 接下来，市场需要关注的，不只是美伊是否恢复谈判或再次交火，还包括霍尔木兹海峡商业航运是否持续受阻、相关油轮事件能否得到独立证实，以及潜在反制是否从军事目标进一步扩展至能源和通信基础设施。 这些因素将共同决定中东风险对国际原油价格及全球供应链的实际冲击。 特朗普暗示再发动小规模军事行动，又称战事可很快结束 据报道，特朗普当地时间周五在佛罗里达州出席集会时表示，美国可能再次对伊朗采取军事行动。他说：“我们可能会再来一次小规模的‘史诗怒火’行动。”特朗普没有进一步说明行动的具体形式、目标或时间安排。 美国国防部将美以2月28日对伊朗发动的军事打击命名为“史诗怒火”行动。特朗普最新的表态意味着，在战争持续近八个月之际，白宫仍未排除进一步动武的可能性。 不过，特朗普周五对结束战争也释放了另一种信号。 据路透社报道，特朗普在白宫南草坪接受记者采访时表示，美国可以很快结束对伊朗的战事，但他同时提出一个问题：美国究竟应该彻底结束战争，还是让冲突逐渐消退？ “我们可以很快结束它，”特朗普说，“问题是，我们要彻底打完，还是就让它慢慢消退？” 特朗普还称，石油正在通过霍尔木兹海峡运输，并表示美国“正在得到我们想要的一切”。但他没有详细说明，如何在维持军事压力的同时确保海峡航运恢复正常。 两种表态并置，凸显出美国当前对伊政策仍存在不确定性：一方面，特朗普希望通过军事和经济压力迫使伊朗让步；另一方面，持续的战争也推高了能源成本，增加了美国国内的政治压力。路透社指出，燃油价格上涨正成为美国11月中期选举前的一项重要政治挑战。 本周美媒称美以制定中选后打击计划，特朗普是否批准仍不确定 特朗普有关可能再次发动军事行动的表态，也令此前有关美以后续军事计划的报道受到关注。 据新华社援引美国《纽约时报》21日周三的报道，美国和以色列军方已制定具体计划，准备在11月美国国会中期选举结束后再次打击伊朗，但特朗普是否会批准实施这一计划尚不确定。 这意味着，军事行动的可能性仍然存在，但不能据此认定美方已经决定在中期选举后发动新一轮打击。 特朗普政府面临的权衡在于：如果继续扩大军事行动，可能进一步打击伊朗的军事能力，却也可能延长冲突、增加海湾地区能源设施遭袭的风险；如果选择结束战争，则需要评估伊朗是否愿意在核计划及地区安全问题上作出实质性让步。 对于能源市场而言，真正影响供应预期的，不仅是是否发动新一轮军事行动，还包括打击范围、伊朗的反制方式，以及冲突是否进一步影响霍尔木兹海峡的商业航运。 伊朗称两艘超级油轮触雷，超450万桶原油涉及其中 霍尔木兹海峡的航运安全风险也在升温。 据央视新闻，当地时间10月23日，伊朗伊斯兰革命卫队海军宣布，两艘试图非法穿越霍尔木兹海峡南部的超级油轮当天早些时候触雷。伊方称，爆炸和大火导致两艘船的机舱瘫痪，船只停泊在原地，船员弃船逃生，两艘油轮合计装载超过450万桶原油。 需要强调的是，这一事件目前应表述为伊朗方面的说法。船只名称、具体受损情况、船员状况以及原油是否发生泄漏，仍需更多独立信息确认，不能将伊方宣称的触雷经过及后果直接视为已经独立证实的事实。 霍尔木兹海峡连接波斯湾与阿曼湾，是全球最重要的能源运输通道之一。即便没有出现大规模、持续性的原油运输中断，油轮遇袭、触雷或被迫改变航线，也可能推高船舶保险费、战争险保费及运输成本。 近期，围绕海峡通行规则的争端持续加剧。伊朗方面曾多次声称，部分船只使用其不认可的航线，并将相关海上事故归因于船只违规通行；美国则持续对伊朗施加海上封锁和经济压力。双方对海峡航行安全及通行规则的立场存在明显分歧。 如果油轮触雷的消息得到进一步证实，且船舶运营商因此减少通过该海域的航次，市场可能重新评估中东原油出口的实际可用规模。不过，事件本身是否造成实质性的供应损失，仍取决于船舶受损程度、货物状态及后续航运情况。 伊朗计划将反制范围扩大至海底通信电缆，基础设施风险外溢 除油轮与能源设施外，伊朗方面据称还在考虑将潜在反制范围扩展至海底通信基础设施。 据路透社10月23日报道，两名伊朗高级安全官员透露，如果美国和以色列再次攻击伊朗，伊朗政府已制定针对海湾地区海底通信电缆的详细计划。两名官员均未披露具体的打击地点或实施方式。 其中一名官员表示，伊朗还可能试图阻止电缆受损后的维修工作，以延长通信中断的时间。该官员警告称，如果伊朗遭到攻击，相关反制将不再受此前所谓“红线”的限制，目标可能从海底电缆延伸至军事基地，包括隐蔽基地。 此前，伊朗伊斯兰革命卫队相关官员已警告，如果伊朗基础设施遭到攻击，霍尔木兹海峡下方的七条主要互联网电缆可能成为打击目标。 不过，海底电缆遭袭的全球影响仍需具体分析。国际电信联盟数据显示，海底电缆承载全球约99%的互联网流量，但电信研究机构TeleGeography研究主管Alan Mauldin表示，经过霍尔木兹海峡的国际带宽占比不到1%，因此即使相关电缆受损，对全球互联网整体的影响也可能有限。海湾地区及依赖相关线路的国家和企业，则可能面临更直接的通信中断风险。 这一威胁的重要性在于，潜在冲突的影响可能不再局限于石油生产、能源设施和海上运输。如果通信电缆也被纳入反制范围，海湾地区的金融交易、企业通信、云服务及跨境数据传输都可能面临额外风险。 但目前报道反映的是伊朗官员所述的预案，并不意味着相关打击已经发生，也不意味着伊朗已经作出实施决定。后续影响仍取决于美伊外交是否继续破裂，以及双方是否进一步扩大军事行动和反制目标。 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。

articles.title: 全球投资级企业债利差创一年半新高，AI融资潮冲击信用市场
articles.summary: 全球信用市场正在发出逾一年来最强烈的避险信号。科技公司为人工智能建设大举举债的前景，叠加油价上涨与法国政局动荡，共同推动全球企业债利差急剧走阔。 彭博指数数据显示， 全球投资级企业债利差周四飙升至129个基点，创2025年5月以来最宽水平。 与此同时， 追踪美国蓝筹企业债违约保护成本的CDX投资级指数周五升至64个基点，触及3月以来高点。亚洲高评级美元债利差也扩至2025年7月以来最高，波动加剧迫使韩国进出口银行推迟一笔日元债券发行。 市场担忧的核心在于：以Meta为代表的科技巨头正在酝酿史无前例的融资规模， 而AI投资能否及时转化为盈利，仍是未知数。 PGIM Credit美国投资级企业债联席主管David Del Vecchio表示，"市场正在消化为AI建设所需潜在发行规模带来的冲击，投资者几乎没有理由主动入场填补空缺。" CreditSights新加坡南亚及东南亚企业债主管Lakshmanan R表示，"我认为这是信用风险更持续性重新定价的开端，是多重全球风险接连冲击市场的共同结果。" Meta巨额支出计划点燃市场忧虑 本轮信用市场动荡的直接导火索，是 Meta本周披露的最新资本支出规划 。 Meta在季度文件中表示，公司正考虑从今秋起的数年内筹集"数千亿美元"资金。其支出承诺已从7月的约7000亿美元攀升至约8250亿美元。 Meta同时在文件中透露，公司特别委员会将抢先锁定资本视为战略要务， 原因是需要"在竞争对手占满各类融资渠道之前"完成融资 ，并将当前形容为"日益具有挑战性的融资环境"。 这一表述进一步加剧了市场对科技公司集中融资、抢占有限资金池的担忧。 SpaceX借债购芯，AI融资规模持续刷新纪录 科技公司的借贷雄心不止于Meta。马斯克旗下SpaceX正寻求筹资400亿美元，用于向英伟达采购芯片，此举将跻身AI建设史上最大规模债务融资之列。 据Semafor援引知情人士报道，此次融资利率将高于SpaceX上次发债时的水平，其中较低评级债券的定价利率约为8.3%。 彭博Trace数据显示，截至周五收盘，SpaceX 2046年到期、票息6.6%的债券利差扩大13个基点至279个基点。 据彭博新闻汇编的数据，今年以来企业在全球债务市场为AI相关支出累计融资逾4500亿美元。Janus Henderson全球多策略及企业信用主管、驻丹佛的John Lloyd预计，明年为AI建设发行的债务总规模或将接近1万亿美元。 市场能否消化？分歧浮现 面对即将到来的万亿美元融资浪潮，市场参与者看法不一。 Lloyd表示， 市场应有能力消化这一规模，投资者对即将到来的融资并非毫无准备。 但他同时警告，市场震荡在所难免："风险已广为人知，因此每一个数据点都可能引发波动，因为它会改变市场对这些风险的权重判断。" 更大的分歧存在于AI投资回报本身。对冲基金巨头Citadel创始人Ken Griffin警告AI存在泡沫风险；黑石总裁Jon Gray则持相反立场，认为需求"几近抛物线式增长"，无需过度担忧。 值得注意的是，尽管利差走阔，美国投资级企业债利差绝对水平仍处于历史相对偏低区间，87个基点明显低于过去十年约109个基点的均值，表明市场整体尚未陷入恐慌。 盈利强劲，或反成风险因子 一个颇具反讽意味的市场逻辑正在形成：科技公司越赚钱，投资者可能越担心。 Meta与SpaceX本周均公布了好于分析师平均预期的业绩，凸显出这些重度借贷者在大规模数据中心等投资尚未完全投产前，已能创造超额利润。 然而，Voya Investment Management美国投资级企业债主管Travis King对此提出了警示。他表示， "指数层面利差尚属收窄，但表面之下已是一片狼藉。如果科技股财报传来好消息，唯一的意涵可能是它们会进一步扩大支出计划。" 这意味着，强劲盈利不仅不会平息市场担忧，反而可能为下一轮更大规模的举债潮埋下伏笔。 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。

articles.title: 西部数据CFO驳斥AI需求见顶论：毫无动摇迹象，若降温反能帮我们追上需求缺口
articles.summary: 西部数据（Western Digital）首席财务官力挺AI存储需求前景，但公司激进的资本支出规划令投资者生疑，周五股价承压。 华尔街见闻提及 ，10月22日Q1财季电话会上，西部数据CFO Kris Sennesael表示， 超大规模云服务商客户"没有任何动摇迹象"，正持续扩大资本开支，并就2030至2031年的供应需求与公司展开讨论。 尽管公司季度业绩超出预期、并上调盈利指引，但资本支出计划的大幅提升盖过了这些利好，引发市场对AI数据中心投资可持续性的担忧。周五西部数据收跌约3%。 当前，存储及其他AI相关板块正面临普遍压力，市场对数据中心及算力基础设施的重投入能否及时转化为回报，疑虑日益升温。 资本支出骤增，自由现金流承压 西部数据在截至近期的财季中，资本支出规模较上年同期增加逾两倍，主要用于扩大高容量硬盘的生产能力。据彭博行业研究数据， 此举导致公司自由现金流利润率收窄约三个百分点。 Sennesael在公司电话会议上表示， 预计资本支出未来五年将维持在营收的4%至6%左右，但未来两年支出将"略高于"这一区间均值 。这一表态触动了市场神经，令部分投资者担忧短期财务弹性受限。 面对外界质疑，Sennesael援引更广泛的客户结构为公司辩护。他指出，超大规模云厂商、新兴云服务商及开发AI模型的前沿实验室均在持续加码存储投资。 他还补充称，即便AI发展势头有所放缓，也可能"有助于公司追上现有需求缺口" ，言下之意是当前供不应求的局面反而构成支撑。 不过，市场研究机构Vital Knowledge在财报后报告中提示， 核心问题仍在于"数据中心支出势头能否维持当前节奏，以及庞大的积压订单能否最终转化为实际营收"。 业绩层面，西部数据表现稳健。公司预测第二财季调整后每股收益最高可达6美元，高于分析师平均预期的4.80美元，超出幅度显著。与此同时，公司将季度股息上调17%，彰显管理层对中期盈利能力的信心。 然而，亮眼的业绩指引未能完全消弭市场对资本支出扩张节奏的疑虑，股价下挫折射出投资者在AI投资回报周期问题上仍存分歧。 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。

articles.title: 高管揭示Meta AI订阅变现新路：Muse免广告但企业服务收费，智能体购物抽成
articles.summary: Meta正试图为AI业务寻找一条不同于传统广告的变现路径。 Meta首席AI官Alexandr Wang在接受日经新闻采访时表示，Meta的个人AI智能体Muse将坚持免广告，普通用户可免费使用，但高阶功能和企业服务将收费，公司还计划从智能体促成的购物交易中抽取佣金。Wang表示，Muse不仅能够回答问题，还可以代替用户执行任务、节省时间和金钱，因此比此前的AI产品更有用。 日经新闻发稿当天、10月23日周五，Muse首次登陆日本市场。Muse 9月8日在北美上线后反响热烈，相关应用下载量六周即达到1000万次，增长速度超过包括ChatGPT在内的部分竞品。 从个人订阅到企业服务，探索广告之外的收入 Alexandr Wang表示，Muse对普通用户免费开放，Meta希望未来将其推广至数十亿用户。不过，对于重度用户，以及希望使用最先进模型的用户，公司已经推出订阅方案。Meta也计划向企业提供付费服务，但Wang没有披露具体的收费标准和推出时间。 与Meta旗下社交平台依靠广告变现的模式不同，Wang明确表示：“Muse内部没有广告，我们也没有投放广告的计划。” 这意味着，至少按照目前的规划，Meta不会直接将广告植入Muse的交互界面。 对于广告收入占比超过95%的Meta而言，Muse的变现路径具有特殊意义。随着产品向更多市场扩张、公司继续投入巨额资金建设AI基础设施，Meta能否将用户增长转化为可持续收入，正成为市场关注的焦点。 智能体购物抽成，探索交易佣金收入 除订阅和企业服务外，Meta还计划从用户通过智能体完成的购物交易中抽取佣金，将Muse从信息和任务助手进一步延伸至消费场景。 这一模式有望让Meta在广告之外获得交易收入，但具体如何落地仍有待观察。 Meta并未公布佣金比例、适用商家范围及正式推出时间，最终收入规模将取决于Muse的任务执行能力、商家接入情况，以及用户是否愿意将购物决策交给智能体。 自有基础设施与安全能力，支撑Muse扩张 Alexandr Wang认为，Meta自有的技术基础设施、安全体系和数据中心，是Muse难以被竞争对手复制的重要优势。对于需要执行任务、处理用户信息并连接不同服务的个人AI智能体而言，模型能力之外，基础设施的规模、可靠性和安全性同样重要。 Meta正在为这套基础设施投入巨额资金。 本周三美股盘后发布财报的同时，Meta公布，最新的2026年资本开支指引区间为1350亿至1450亿美元，将指引区间的低端上调50亿美元。 周四，Meta还在递交监管文件中披露，截至9月底，公司未开始履行租赁义务和不可撤销合同承诺合计约8100亿美元，若计入最高约147亿美元的或有云计算容量采购义务，未来承诺投入总额升至接近8250亿美元。 上述投入既服务于Meta现有业务，也将支持新一代AI模型和产品开发。基础设施能否转化为更强的产品能力，并进一步带动订阅、企业服务和交易佣金收入，将是Muse商业化能否取得进展的关键。 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。

articles.title: 报道：德国10月达成协议以来首次启动招标，出售战略储备中的柴油、取暖油和原油
articles.summary: 德国正从战略储备两端同步发力：既向市场释放石油，又斥资锁定冬季天然气供应，折射出欧洲最大经济体在能源安全层面持续承压的现实。 10月23日周五， 德国石油储备机构EBV发出招标邀请，拟出售战略储备中的柴油、取暖油及原油 。据路透社， 这是德国自G7国家10月初达成协调放储协议以来的首次实际执行。 与此同时，德国天然气市场运营商Trading Hub Europe（THE）披露， 为保障冬季供应安全，德国已斥资近2.45亿欧元（约2.74亿美元）签订额外供气合同，背景是当前德国天然气库存水平较去年同期大幅偏低。 两项举措同日公布，显示德国在油气领域均面临供应侧压力，市场关注的焦点将集中于此次石油招标的最终成交量，以及天然气库存能否在入冬前得到有效补充。 石油放储：G7协议落地，德国率先执行 据路透社，EBV于周五向相关企业分别发出购买邀请，涉及产品涵盖柴油、取暖油及原油。 由于各企业收到的邀约数量不同，此次招标的总规模暂无法得到确认 ，EBV亦未在正常工作时间内回应路透社的置评请求。 此次放储是G7国家10月初协调行动的组成部分。彼时，在美国总统特朗普的压力下，柴油价格高企已成为11月3日美国中期选举的重要政治议题，G7国家同意从紧急储备中释放共计1亿桶石油。 该协议由国际能源署（IEA）统筹协调，其中包括优先释放2000万桶柴油，以及3月伊朗战争爆发时承诺释放但尚未动用的剩余储量。 德国经济部长Katherina Reiche本月早些时候表示， 德国承诺释放至多1500万桶柴油、取暖油及原油，是欧洲国家中出资规模最大的 ，但未披露具体时间表。 德国联邦参议院上周已为放储扫清立法障碍，将法定最低储备要求从90天消费量临时下调至82天。 从市场影响来看，欧洲基准柴油期货较原油期货的溢价9月底曾触及每桶95美元的历史高位，截至周五已回落至约76美元。 此次德国向市场注入额外柴油与取暖油，预计将对西北欧裂解价差及内陆产品升水形成压制，原油部分的市场影响相对有限。 天然气储备：库存告急，专项合同护航冬季 天然气方面，形势同样不容乐观。THE数据显示， 截至10月21日，德国天然气储存设施的充填率仅为61.1%，远低于去年同期的75.4%。 为应对这一缺口，THE已通过标准招标及专项招标两条渠道合计签订约2.45亿欧元的供气合同。 其中，专门针对2027年2月和3月供应保障的特别招标耗资约1.07亿欧元，叠加每年例行用于解决管网瓶颈的约1.37亿欧元标准招标合同。 THE表示，这些合同的设计逻辑在于为参与企业提供激励，促使其将天然气在储库中保留更长时间，并可能存入额外量，相当于一种针对潜在供应短缺的"保险机制"。 当前库存水平与去年同期近15个百分点的差距，使得上述安排的紧迫性显著提升，也令德国能否顺利渡过即将到来的冬季供暖季成为市场持续关注的变量。 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。
